## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.94961.2.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.94961.2.sa3)

Summary:

In order to study the factors and neural dynamics that lead to the suppression of irrelevant information in the brain, the authors trained artificial neural networks in the execution of a task that involved the discrimination of complex stimuli with three main features: color, shape, and width. Specific combinations of color and shape led to a reward, but the temporal structure made color dynamically irrelevant at the beginning of the trial, and then it became relevant once the shape was presented. On the other hand, the width of the stimulus was always irrelevant. Importantly, non-human primates were also trained to execute this task (in a previous study by the authors) and the activity from neural populations from the dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (dlPFC) was recorded, allowing to compare the coding of information by the artificial neural network model with what happens in biological neural populations.

The authors changed systematically the amount of noise present in the neural network model, as well as limiting the firing rate of the artificial neurons to simulate the limitations imposed by high metabolic costs in biological neurons. They found that models with medium and low noise, as well as medium and low metabolic cost, developed information encoding patterns that resembled the patterns observed throughout learning in the dlPFC, as follows: early in the learning process, color information was strongly represented during the whole trial, as well as shape and width, whereas the color/shape combination significance (XOR operation) was weakly encoded. Late in learning, color information was initially suppressed (while it was deemed irrelevant) and became more prominent during the shape presentation. Width information coding decreased, and the XOR operation result became more strongly encoded.

Subthreshold activity dynamics were studied by training artificial networks consisting of 2 neurons, with the aim of understanding how dynamically irrelevant information is suppressed and then encoded more strongly at a different time during the trial. Under medium noise and medium metabolic cost, color information is suppressed by the divergence of the activity away from the level that triggers spikes. The authors claim that this subthreshold dynamic explains the suppression of irrelevant information in biological neural networks.

Strengths:

The study leverages the power of computational models to simulate biological networks and do manipulations that are difficult (if not impossible) to perform in vivo. The analyses of the activity of the network model are neat and thorough and provide a clear demonstration of how noise and metabolic costs may affect the information coding in the brain. The mathematical analyses are rigorous and nicely documented.

Weaknesses:

The study does not leverage the fact that they have access to the activity of individual neurons both on a neural network model and in neural recordings. The model/brain comparison results are limited to the decodability of different pieces of information during the execution of the task at different stages of learning. It would have been useful if the authors had shown response profiles of individual neurons, both biological and artificial, to strengthen the claim that the activity patterns are similar. Perhaps showing that the firing rates vary in a similar way in the large models (like they do for the 2-neuron model) would have been informative. For instance, it is possible that suppression is not occurring in the dlPFC, but that the PFC receives input with this information already suppressed. If suppression indeed happens in the PFC, response profiles associated with this process may be observed.

There is no way to say that the 2-neuron models are in any way informative of what happens in brain neurons, or even larger artificial networks since the sources of sensory input, noise, and inhibition will differ between biological and artificial networks. And because the firing patterns are not shown for large networks, it is not clear if some non-coding artificial neurons will become broadly inhibitory but maintain a relatively high firing rate (to mention only one possibility).

results.result: Task-optimized recurrent neural networks exhibit a range of representational strategies depending on noise level (σ) and firing rate regularization (λ). Networks with low noise and low regularization show maximal representation (high decodability of all stimuli including irrelevant width), while networks with medium noise and medium regularization show minimal representation (weak decodability of irrelevant stimuli). Statically irrelevant stimuli (width) are more strongly suppressed than dynamically irrelevant stimuli (color) across all parameter regimes.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C41 provide comprehensive computational evidence from systematic parameter sweeps (Figure 2) showing how noise and regularization affect stimulus decodability. The grid search over parameter values (C34-C38) demonstrates robust patterns, and the asymmetry between static and dynamic irrelevance (C39) is well-documented. The observation that pure chance-level decoding is never achieved (C40-C41) is appropriately noted as a limitation.

results.result: Neural recordings from primate lateral PFC over the course of learning show that representations change in line with a minimal representational strategy. XOR decodability significantly increased during the shape period, while color decodability significantly decreased during the color period (when irrelevant) and width decodability significantly decreased during the shape period. Recordings spanned the entire learning process from first exposure to the task.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 provide direct experimental evidence from 376 neurons across 27 sessions in two monkeys (C42). The key strength is that recordings commenced from first task exposure (C43), allowing genuine learning-related changes to be observed. Statistical significance is reported for the critical changes in irrelevant stimulus coding (C48, C49), supporting the minimal representational strategy interpretation.

results.result: Networks trained with medium noise and medium regularization (σ_m, λ_m) show learning-related changes in stimulus decodability that closely match the experimental PFC data. XOR decodability significantly increased after shape onset, color decodability significantly decreased during the color period, and width decodability significantly decreased during the shape period.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 demonstrate that the σ_m, λ_m parameter regime produces the best qualitative match to experimental data (Figure 3b). The parallel structure of changes across XOR, color, and width decodability between model and data provides strong support. However, the evaluation notes some quantitative differences (C57, C100-C101) that are appropriately discussed as limitations.

results.result: Mathematical analysis of a simplified linear model reveals that maximizing task performance requires strong relevant coding, weak irrelevant coding, and small overlap, while minimizing metabolic cost requires both relevant and irrelevant coding to be weak. Performance decreases with both noise (σ) and regularization (λ), while relevant coding strength shows a non-monotonic relationship with σ. These theoretical predictions are confirmed by recurrent neural network simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C67 present a coherent theoretical framework (Appendix 1, Figure 4) that is validated by computational simulations (Figure 4e-g). The mathematical analysis provides mechanistic insight into the trade-offs between performance and metabolic cost. The confirmation of theoretical predictions in full RNN simulations (C67) strengthens the conclusions, though the simplified model necessarily omits some complexities of the full task.

results.result: Both in lPFC recordings and optimized recurrent networks (σ_m, λ_m regime), the strength of relevant (XOR) coding increased significantly over learning while irrelevant (width) coding decreased significantly. Relevant and irrelevant directions remained strongly orthogonal throughout learning with no significant change in overlap.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 provide convergent evidence from both experimental data and computational models (Figure 4h-i) for the key geometric properties of neural representations. The statistical tests show significant changes in coding strength but not in orthogonality. The parallel findings across data and model strengthen the conclusions, though the lack of change in overlap (C70-C71) may reflect the specific stimulus structure used.

results.result: The suppression of dynamically irrelevant stimuli (color during the color period) is achieved through activity-silent, sub-threshold dynamics. In medium noise-medium regularization networks, color inputs drive neural activity into the rectified (negative) part of the ReLU nonlinearity during the color period, resulting in zero firing rates and no metabolic cost, while still allowing the information to be used later in the trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 provide a mechanistic explanation for dynamic irrelevance suppression through detailed analysis of two-neuron networks (Figure 5a-d). The mechanism is clearly demonstrated: color inputs become negative (driving activity below threshold) in σ_m, λ_m networks but not in σ_l, λ_l networks. This explains both the weak early color decoding and the zero metabolic cost during the color period. The mechanism is biologically plausible and computationally verified.

results.result: In lPFC recordings, firing rates decreased significantly over learning in all task periods, with the largest decreases during fixation and color periods. After learning, firing rates during the color period were not significantly higher than during fixation, but increased significantly during the shape period compared to fixation.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 provide experimental validation of the activity-silent mechanism predicted by the models (Figure 5f). The pattern of firing rate changes—particularly the lack of increase from fixation to color period after learning—is consistent with sub-threshold dynamics during the dynamically irrelevant color period. Statistical significance is reported for the key comparisons.

results.result: Different settings of biologically relevant hyperparameters (noise and metabolic cost) yield qualitatively different dynamical regimes. Increasing noise and regularization leads to greater filtering of irrelevant information, consistent with known PFC properties and findings in other brain regions including motor cortex and grid cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C94 synthesize the main findings and place them in broader context through extensive citations (C87, C89, C91-C94). The generalization to other brain regions is supported by prior literature showing similar effects of regularization in motor cortex and spatial navigation systems. However, the predictions about generalization (C88, C90) remain to be directly tested.

results.result: The experimental task consists of fixation, color, shape, and reward periods. Reward is delivered according to an XOR relationship between color and shape. Width is a statically irrelevant stimulus dimension (never predictive of reward), while color is dynamically irrelevant (irrelevant during the color period but relevant during the shape period).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 clearly describe the task structure (Figure 1a-b). The distinction between static irrelevance (width) and dynamic irrelevance (color) is well-defined and central to the study's design. The task structure is straightforward and the definitions are internally consistent.

results.result: Two adult male rhesus macaques performed the task with neural recordings from ventral and dorsal lPFC commencing from first task exposure. The dataset comprised 376 neurons across 27 sessions, with trials containing fixation errors excluded. Firing rates were computed by convolving spike trains with a 50ms Gaussian kernel.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C136 provide essential methodological details about the experimental dataset. The key strength is that recordings began from first exposure (C131), which is critical for studying learning-related changes. Sample sizes and data processing steps are clearly specified. The note that the experiment was performed once in two animals (C136) is an important limitation for generalizability.

results.result: Cognitive flexibility requires encoding task-relevant and ignoring task-irrelevant stimuli, but mechanisms for ignoring irrelevant stimuli remain poorly understood. Complex tasks involve multiple stimulus types including statically irrelevant stimuli (always irrelevant) and dynamically irrelevant stimuli (relevant at some times but not others). How these should be represented for optimal performance remains an open question.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 establish the scientific context and motivation. These are well-supported by citations to prior literature (C6, C8, C9) and represent accurate characterizations of the field's current understanding. The definitions of static vs. dynamic irrelevance are clear and well-grounded in previous work.

results.result: Neural noise and metabolic costs affect stimulus representations in neural circuits, but models typically explore only a limited range of these biologically relevant parameters. This limited exploration may mean we are recovering only a few of many possible representational strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 are well-supported by extensive citations (C14-C17) and provide important motivation for the systematic parameter exploration conducted in this study. The critique of limited hyperparameter exploration in prior work (C17-C18) is fair and well-documented.

results.result: Metabolic cost was operationalized through L2 firing rate regularization, which penalizes high overall firing rates. Although L2 regularization is generally considered weaker than L1, it still encouraged networks to use sub-threshold activity. Alternative operationalizations exist, including L1 regularization (promoting sparsity) and synaptic weight regularization.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 clearly describe the modeling choices with appropriate citations (C108, C110, C112-C113). The observation that L2 regularization produced sub-threshold dynamics (C111) is an interesting empirical finding. The discussion of alternatives (C110, C112-C113) appropriately acknowledges other possible approaches.

results.result: High-dimensional representations enable flexible behavior by allowing many behavioral readouts, while low-dimensional representations are more robust to noise and allow generalization. Prolonged exposure to tasks with limited stimulus conditions may encourage low-dimensional dynamics, while tasks with rich, varied stimuli may lead to high-dimensional representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 present reasonable hypotheses supported by citations (C95-C96), but the predictions about task structure effects (C97-C98) are speculative. While the logic is sound, these claims about how task structure determines dimensionality require direct experimental testing across different task types.

results.result: Some differences between model and data (e.g., shape decodability decreasing while color decodability increased during the shape period) may reflect fundamental differences in how brains encode sensory information upstream of PFC compared to the abstract inputs used in models. Width was very strongly represented in early learning and maintained high cross-generalized decoding even after learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C107 appropriately acknowledge limitations in the model-data correspondence. The speculation about upstream sensory encoding differences (C101-C102, C104) is reasonable and supported by neuroscience literature (C102). The observation about width's strong representation (C105-C106) is data-driven. The methodological point about focusing on changes rather than absolute levels (C107) is a reasonable approach to these limitations.

results.result: Previous studies of learning-related changes in PFC typically used reversal-learning paradigms where animals were already task-proficient. Studies in mice and rats showed that PFC neurons adjust selectivity to suppress currently irrelevant information. In monkeys, PFC dimensionality increased as novel stimulus values were learned, but representations only distinguished stimuli after values were learned, not upon first exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C121 accurately characterize prior work through appropriate citations (C114-C118). The distinction between the current study (recordings from first exposure) and prior work (recordings after proficiency) is important and well-articulated (C114, C121). These claims provide appropriate context for understanding the novelty of the current approach.

results.result: Recent studies have examined how different hyperparameter settings affect network solutions, including effects of weight regularization on sequential dynamics, effects of nonlinearity saturation on functional clustering, and effects of noise and regularization on grid cell-like properties. Various hyperparameters including nonlinearity type and weight initialization affect representational strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C127 provide comprehensive context about related computational work through extensive citations (C123-C126). The synthesis across different domains (working memory, path integration, motor control) strengthens the argument that hyperparameter effects are a general phenomenon. The conclusion about the importance of studying learning-biological constraint interactions (C127) follows logically.

results.result: Currently irrelevant stimuli may become relevant in future tasks, and it's unclear whether dynamically irrelevant stimuli should be suppressed since the information is ultimately needed. Stimuli may be strongly represented a priori if previously important, and representing a stimulus may be prerequisite for learning its relevance. Studying changes over learning (rather than post-learning snapshots) provides insights into how tasks affect representational strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C22 present logical inferences about learning and representation (C11-C12, C19-C20) supported by citations where appropriate (C20, C22). The characterization of limitations in prior experimental approaches (C21) is accurate. These claims effectively motivate the study's focus on learning-related changes.

results.result: For stimuli more similar than the XOR and width features studied here, the overlap between relevant and irrelevant features may decrease over learning rather than remaining small.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is pure speculation about what might happen with different stimulus types. While the hypothesis is reasonable, there is no data in the current study to support or refute it. This represents an interesting direction for future work but cannot be evaluated as supported or unsupported based on the current evidence.

results.result: The results should generalize to richer, more complex cognitive tasks requiring context switching or working memory.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is a prediction about generalization that, while supported by citations showing irrelevant information filtering in such tasks (C89), has not been directly tested in this study. The prediction is reasonable but remains speculative until tested with actual context-switching or working memory tasks.

results.result: RNNs trained with varying levels of noise and firing rate regularization exhibit different representational strategies. Networks with low noise and low regularization represent all stimuli including irrelevant ones (C30-C31), while networks with medium noise and medium regularization employ a minimal representational strategy that weakly represents irrelevant stimuli (C33). Statically irrelevant stimuli (width) are more strongly suppressed than dynamically irrelevant stimuli (color) across all parameter settings (C39).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as a valuable contribution. The editor states the work 'provides a valuable analysis of the effect of two commonly used hyperparameters, noise amplitude and firing rate regularization, on the representations of relevant and irrelevant stimuli.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The article provides a valuable analysis of the effect of two parameters on representations of irrelevant stimuli in trained RNNs.' Reviewer 3 states 'The analyses of the activity of the network model are neat and thorough and provide a clear demonstration of how noise and metabolic costs may affect the information coding in the brain.'

results.result: Neural recordings from primate PFC show that over learning, XOR (task-relevant) decodability increases (C45), while color decodability during the color period (when dynamically irrelevant) and width decodability (statically irrelevant) both decrease (C48-C49). The strength of relevant coding increases while irrelevant coding decreases (C68-C69), consistent with a minimal representational strategy (C4).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these neural recording findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes 'The neural data showed systematic changes in the representations of these features and of the expected reward as the learning progressed.' The editor acknowledges the work is 'based on comparisons to previously published data from the same lab.' No reviewer questions the validity of these learning-related changes in PFC activity.

results.result: Medium noise-medium regularization RNNs show learning-related changes qualitatively similar to PFC: XOR decodability increases (C52), color decodability during the color period decreases (C54), and width decodability decreases (C55), while shape and color decodability during the shape period remain stable (C53).
results.evaluation: Reviewers express significant concerns about the model-data match. The editor states 'The evidence indicating that the mechanisms identified in the RNNs are the same ones operating in PFC was considered incomplete.' Reviewer 1 notes 'The match between the real PFC and the model networks is highly qualitative' and 'comparisons only make sense in terms of *changes* between early and late learning. The time scales, activity levels, and decoding accuracies involved are all different.' Reviewer 2 states 'The change in dynamics of 'color' representations in the prefrontal cortex only qualitatively matches RNN dynamics and may arise from other causes.'

results.result: The mechanism for suppressing dynamically irrelevant stimuli involves activity-silent, sub-threshold dynamics (C5). In medium noise-medium regularization networks, color inputs drive sub-threshold activity into the negative quadrant during the color period, producing zero firing rate activity (C78) and representing color information in an activity-silent state (C79-C80).
results.evaluation: Reviewers express substantial concerns about this mechanistic claim. Reviewer 2 states 'The mechanism for suppressing dynamically relevant stimuli appears to be incomplete and does not explain clearly enough how representations of 'color' which are suppressed through negative input weights become un-suppressed in the presence of the second variable 'shape'.' Reviewer 3 notes 'There is no way to say that the 2-neuron models are in any way informative of what happens in brain neurons, or even larger artificial networks' and 'because the firing patterns are not shown for large networks, it is not clear if some non-coding artificial neurons will become broadly inhibitory but maintain a relatively high firing rate.'

results.result: In PFC recordings, firing rates decreased significantly over learning in all task periods (C81), with the decrease most substantial during fixation and color periods. After learning, firing rates during the color period were not significantly higher than fixation (C82), but increased significantly during the shape period (C83).
results.evaluation: These firing rate findings from neural recordings are not challenged by reviewers. They are presented as empirical observations that support the metabolic cost interpretation, though reviewers question whether the interpretation is the only possible explanation.

results.result: Mathematical analyses show that maximizing task performance requires strong relevant coding, weak irrelevant coding, and small overlap (C58), while reducing metabolic cost requires both relevant and irrelevant coding to be weak (C59). The analyses predict how noise (σ) and regularization (λ) affect performance, metabolic cost, and coding strength (C60-C66), predictions confirmed by RNN simulations (C67).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the mathematical analyses without challenge. Reviewer 3 states 'The mathematical analyses are rigorous and nicely documented.' Reviewer 1 notes 'The simulations and theoretical calculations indicated that the changes in PFC activity...can be understood as an attempt by the circuitry to use an efficient representational strategy.' No reviewer questions the validity of the mathematical framework itself.

results.result: Differences between model and PFC data may arise from fundamentally different ways brains encode sensory information upstream of PFC compared to abstract sensory inputs in models (C57, C101). Width was very strongly represented in early learning in PFC (C105-C106), possibly because it is a more potent sensory feature (C104). Studying changes in decoding over learning rather than absolute levels helps focus on learning-related features independent of upstream representations (C107).
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept this explanation for model-data differences. Reviewer 1 explicitly notes this limitation: 'The match between the real PFC and the model networks is highly qualitative, and as noted by the authors, comparisons only make sense in terms of *changes* between early and late learning.' This acknowledgment by reviewers indicates acceptance of the authors' reasoning about why absolute comparisons are problematic.

results.result: Metabolic cost was operationalized through L2 firing rate regularization (C108-C109), which penalizes high overall firing rates. Although L2 is generally weaker than L1 regularization, it still encouraged purely sub-threshold activity (C111). Alternative operationalizations like L1 regularization, weight regularization, or sub-threshold activity regularization are also biologically plausible (C110, C112-C113).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 directly challenges the metabolic cost interpretation: 'Interpretation of results in terms of the effect of metabolic cost on cortical dynamics is not backed up by the presented data/analyses. The change in dynamics of 'color' representations in the prefrontal cortex only qualitatively matches RNN dynamics and may arise from other causes.' This indicates the reviewers are uncertain whether the L2 regularization truly captures metabolic constraints or whether other factors could explain the results.

This represents a key disagreement on the strength of model-data correspondence.
